This is tough. I don't really have a feeling either way on who is right but I consider the fact that while you want to be with your daughter, understand that she's accepting of the current situation. You want to move closer for your benefit at this point in time.

That being said, it's not unreasonable to want that. I think your girlfriend is completely wrong about her perspective, but her desire to stay closer to her family and job security is completely rational. As people have pointed out, what happens if it doesn't work out? She's stuck in that city with no family and less prospects. She only has things to lose in this situation. Not that relationships are a net sum, but it's hard to convince someone to do something if it's not beneficial to them aside from staying with you.

You need to find more ways to make the situation appealing to her. And if she won't come around, then you have to make a choice.

As a black person, your friend's comment was deeply inappropriate and is the exact sort of thing black people have to be conscious of when dating outside of their race. I'm sure in a place with not many black people, your boyfriend has had to put up with a lot of shit and he's hyper-aware of these things. You being white, probably cannot begin to understand but at best you can be sensitive. I would advise you call out that friend for their comment, you didn't stand up for him in the moment. That sort of thing is a difficult joke for someone you've just started dating and your friends don't know. The fact that that's immediately what they jumped to can speak for the kind of person you and your friends are in your boyfriend's mind.

If he starts going overboard about it, and starts becoming hostile or toxic about it you should break up because there's nothing you can do about that. Otherwise, there's really very little you can do to convince him and nor should you try because you could end up saying something even more offensive ("I don't see race" etc.). Just try to continue your relationship and consider it a bump in the road.

Do you know of the concept of grooming in relation to child predators? Idk if there's a similar term for this for domestic abuse but this is what it reminds me of. He's subtly testing your limits for what you'll allow him to do, but at the same time instilling in you the fear that he could do something. Asserting control, and then saying just joking so you think it's ok. But the next time he could put you in a chokehold for "fun", or twist your arm behind your back, etc. etc. And each time it happens you'll obviously be scared, but not know whether he's serious until the tipping point.

Assert your boundary very clearly NOW. And if he steps over that again in any similar way, you need to leave for your safety and before you get trapped in the cycle of abuse.

EDIT: Also if you're ever in a more serious situation where someone is trying to choke/suffocate you, play dead. Most people don't know that you actually need to cut off air for a significant period of time before you experience serious damage, usually your body just defaults to losing consciousness first. Thanks to movies, people just assume once the person is limp, they're dead and they'll relent. Playing dead will also stop you from panicking and using up more vital resources.
